name: The Errand
description: Four optional checks around a simple collection run into the city. None of them gate the scene and none of them cost anything on a failure -- same zero-stakes rule as The Road In and Kit Issue. The scene's actual content is the conversation with the old man, and that is reached by talking to him, never by passing a check.

checks.name: Find somebody who can read the docket

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, no adjustment -- offered to the whole table, not a specialist's roll

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Third person they ask points straight across the street. "Old fella in the tea house. He used to be something, I think."
outcomes.success: A few wrong turns, then somebody mentions the tea house.
outcomes.failure: Nobody in the quarter knows, and several are cheerfully certain the docket is a misprint. They find him anyway -- he is sitting where he always sits, and he has been watching six lost trainees for ten minutes with open interest.
outcomes.criticalFailure: As failure, and one of the people they asked will remember six Directorate trainees asking odd questions. Nothing comes of it tonight.

checks.name: Take a proper look at him

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step hard -- most of the table won't get this, and that's the point

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Everything below, and the thing that matters: he notices being looked at, and he is not used to it. Whatever else happens in this scene, he has decided he likes this one.
outcomes.success: A chemist, and not a recent one. Old stains at the first and second fingers that no longer wash out. He reads the docket the way a musician reads music -- he is not working it out, he is hearing it. Poor, and careful about not looking it. His coat has been mended well, by hand, more than once.
outcomes.failure: An old man in a tea house. Nothing else.
outcomes.criticalFailure: An old man in a tea house, and a faint conviction that he is nobody at all. Do not correct it.

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step hard -- matches a-mark-at-head-height in c1s1-the-road-in exactly, on purpose

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Same deep violet, same neat hand, same height. And this one is on the wall people face while they queue for the store -- not on the road side, where it would be seen by traffic. It is placed for standing crowds.
outcomes.success: The same mark they may have seen on the way in. Same colour, same height. Somebody has been doing this for a while.

checks.name: Get anything at all out of the storekeeper

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step easy -- this is a treat, not a test

outcomes.criticalSuccess: She finds the item in under a minute once she knows what it actually is, throws in something small she can't sell, and tells them which of the three chandlers on this stretch waters their primer.
outcomes.success: Cheerful, unhurried, and completely unable to help until somebody tells her what the docket means.
outcomes.failure: She has a queue, they are six teenagers in brand-new uniforms, and the docket is somebody else's problem.
outcomes.criticalFailure: As failure, and she calls them 'the Directorate' for the rest of the scene, in the tone you'd use for a utility company.

notes:
NONE OF THESE REACH MANAKO, DELIBERATELY. The docket's obsolete catalogue name is not decodable by a level-1 character at any DC -- it is a dead naming convention, not a hard knowledge check, so there is no roll that lets the party skip the old man. read-the-old-man is the only check that touches him at all, and what it buys is warmth, not information.

The contact route he offers at the end of the scene is NOT gated on a check either. It is earned by talking to him like a person. A table that rolls badly and is kind still gets it; a table that rolls well and treats him as a vending machine does not. That is the whole design of the scene and it should not be turned into a skill gate.
